notes.meaning: God reminds Joshua that he has reached an advanced age, likely around one hundred years old. Although major campaigns had broken the power of the Canaanite kings, large stretches of territory were still not conquered or settled. God tells him his time for leading active warfare is over, and he must now turn to dividing the land among the tribes before he dies.

God spells out the southwestern regions that Israel had not yet subdued. These lands included the coastal strip held by the five Philistine city-lords, along with the territory of the Geshurites and the Avvites near Egypt. Even though the Philistines were not descendants of Canaan, their territory was counted as part of Canaan and marked out for Israel.

God lists the unconquered northern and coastal areas. This included the Phoenician territory near Sidon, the fortress of Aphek, the land around the seaport city of Gebal, and the Lebanon mountains eastward to Lebo-hamath. These vast northern borders showed Israel how much more land God was willing to give them beyond what they already held.

God promises that He Himself will drive out these remaining enemies if Israel continues to obey Him. Joshua is instructed not to wait until every corner is subdued, but to distribute all the land by casting lots right away. Allotting the unconquered territory tested their faith and gave each tribe the duty to step out and possess its own portion.

Before Joshua divides the western territory, the account confirms what Moses had already given to Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh on the east side of the Jordan River. Joshua leaves Moses' work undisturbed, honouring what God's servant had established. This southern section of the eastern lands stretched from the Arnon gorge north through the tableland and covered the cities once ruled by King Sihon.

The eastern allotment also included the region of Gilead, Mount Hermon, and the entire kingdom of Og in Bashan up to Salecah. Og was the last surviving giant king from the ancient Rephaim people. Moses had defeated these kings and taken their land so that Israel could settle there.

Israel failed to expel the native peoples of Geshur and Maacath in the far north of the Transjordan. Because the tribes stopped short in their warfare and grew content with what they had, these foreign kingdoms remained living among them. In later generations, leaving these groups undisturbed brought snares and trouble to Israel.

The tribe of Levi received no large province or territorial land like the other tribes. Instead, their livelihood was provided through the sacrificial offerings and tithes brought to God by the other tribes. Having God's sanctuary service as their life's work was a higher honour and provision than owning farmland.

Moses divided the land among the families of Reuben, giving them the southern portion of the Transjordan. Their border started at the deep Arnon Valley and took in the high plateau, reaching Heshbon and nearby towns. Setting down these exact borders prevented future property quarrels and preserved a record of God's faithful provision.

Reuben's lot included several fortified towns, desert border garrisons, and fertile agricultural areas known for their vineyards. It also took in the slopes of Mount Pisgah, where Moses looked over the Promised Land before his death, and Beth-peor nearby. Every specific town was named to ensure that each family's boundaries were clear and peaceful.

The record mentions how Sihon fell in battle, along with five Midianite chiefs who ruled under his authority. It also recalls the execution of Balaam the pagan fortune-teller, who had tried to curse Israel and led them into sin with Midian. God's righteous judgment caught up with everyone who actively fought against His people.

The western boundary of Reuben's territory reached the edge of the Jordan River. This note concludes the list of walled cities and surrounding rural settlements assigned to the clans of Reuben. God gave them a secure homeland after their many decades of wandering in the wilderness.

Gad was given the land north of Reuben, covering the southern half of Gilead and land that King Sihon had earlier seized from Ammon. Israel did not steal Ammonite land, because Moses only took what Sihon already occupied by conquest. Their borders stretched north from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh and eastward toward Mahanaim.

Gad's territory ran northward along the low valley of the Jordan River all the way to the Sea of Chinnereth, known later as the Sea of Galilee. It included ancient sites like Succoth, where Jacob had once camped, along with several other key towns and farming hamlets. This completed the formal public record of Gad's family inheritance.

The eastern half of the tribe of Manasseh received the northernmost Transjordan territory, beginning at Mahanaim and covering all of Bashan. This wealthy region included sixty towns captured and settled by Jair, a bold leader from their tribe. God rewarded this family clan with a vast and fertile grazing land.

Half of Gilead and the former capital cities of King Og were given to the descendants of Machir, the warlike son of Manasseh. Moses granted this area to them because of their bravery in driving out the previous inhabitants. This territory formed the northern outpost of Israel east of the Jordan.

This verse sums up the division of the land east of the Jordan, which Moses had settled while the camp was stationed on the plains of Moab opposite Jericho. It serves as an official close to the Transjordan allotments before the book turns to Joshua dividing the west. Moses' faithful leadership was thereby honoured and kept intact.

The chapter ends by repeating that Levi received no tract of land of their own. Instead of owning an earthly territory, the Lord Himself was their portion and provider as they carried out the priestly service. True security and wealth for God's servants come from belonging to the Lord rather than from accumulating worldly possessions.
